item.title: How Does Postgres Store Data?
item.description:
How Does Postgres Store Data?

As we all know, postgres is an awesome, open source database system. In these series of blog posts, I am going to explore some internals of Postgres.

In this post, we explore how postgres internally organizes and stores data that we expect it to store.

Prerequisites

For this ( and subsequent ) posts, I am assuming that the reader:

  • Knows what docker containers are, how to build and run them.
  • Is familiar with the terms processes, threads, and virtual memory

For this post, I am using a docker container for postgres and a docker container for a simple application connecting to postgres. Both files can be found here.

To build the containers, run:

# Build the postgres and the python application images
docker build -t postgres-17.6:v1 .
docker build -f Dockerfile.client -t pg-client:v1 .

# To let the python app talk to postgres, we create a docker network
docker network create pgnet

# Run the docker container for postgres
docker run -d --name postgres --network pgnet -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres-17.6:v1

# Run the docker container for the python application

Storage in Postgres

Before we start the actual exploration, note that in the Dockerfile, we have created a user myuser and a database mydatabase in our postgres server.

Now, let’s create a table in our database so that we can insert some data. Let’s exec into the postgres container using:

docker exec -it postgres bash

Once inside, we can do: psql -U myuser -d mydatabase. This opens a client connection to mydatabase using myuser. From the postgres server point of view, this is just another connection. Now we can create the table and insert some data as:

CREATE TABLE mytable (id INT, name TEXT);

INSERT INTO mytable VALUES (1, 'Alice');

We receive a response from the postgres server saying that the insert was successfully done. Postgres has successfully persisted this data onto disk. But what does it mean to “persist data on disk”? At the end of the day, these are simply files! Whatever data we insert is stored in some file, in some directory created by the postgres server.

We can do SHOW data_directory; to get the directory path where the data files are stored. I see /var/lib/postgresql/data as the output. On most Linux/Docker based containers, this is going to be the path unless configured differently. Let’s get into this directory and see what’s there:

# First close the client connection and get out of psql
exit

cd /var/lib/postgresql/data
ls -l

We see the following output:

postgres@7997d00b7436:~/data$ ls -l
total 128
drwx------ 6 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 base
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 global
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_commit_ts
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_dynshmem
-rw------- 1 postgres postgres  5743 Mar 14 13:05 pg_hba.conf
-rw------- 1 postgres postgres  2640 Mar 14 13:05 pg_ident.conf
drwx------ 4 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_logical
drwx------ 4 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_multixact
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_notify
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_replslot
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_serial
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_snapshots
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_stat
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_stat_tmp
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_subtrans
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_tblspc
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_twophase
-rw------- 1 postgres postgres     3 Mar 14 13:05 PG_VERSION
drwx------ 4 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_wal
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres  4096 Mar 14 13:05 pg_xact
-rw------- 1 postgres postgres    88 Mar 14 13:05 postgresql.auto.conf
-rw------- 1 postgres postgres 30777 Mar 14 13:05 postgresql.conf
-rw------- 1 postgres postgres    36 Mar 14 13:05 postmaster.opts
-rw------- 1 postgres postgres    94 Mar 14 13:05 postmaster.pid

Already we see there are some files and directories present in this. You can check what these files contain by doing: cat <filename>. Mostly these are configuration files that we’re not going to get into now. We’re also not going to touch any other directories than base. Each is a separate blog post on its own!

If we do, cd /base/ && ls -l, we see several subdirectories named after some numbers:

postgres@7997d00b7436:~/data$ cd base/ && ls -l
total 16
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres 4096 Mar 14 13:08 1
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres 4096 Mar 14 13:05 16385
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres 4096 Mar 14 13:05 4
drwx------ 2 postgres postgres 4096 Mar 14 13:07 5

These numbers are called Object IDs or OIDs in Postgres. Every object that postgres creates- table, index, function, role, database, anything - gets an OID. These subdirectories are data directories for each of the database that we have in our postgres server. There are some default databases and there is one database that we have created.

Each of these directories are going to contain some files containing the data of the tables in the database and some files for additional metadata for efficiency. Let’s find out which of these directories is for mydatabase.

# Connect to postgres server as a client
psql -U myuser -d mydatabase

SELECT oid, datname FROM pg_database;

I see that mydatabase has an OID of 16385. This number might be different for you. There are other default and template databases as well, which we don’t have to worry about for now. exit this connection.

Now, we can cd into the directory for our database and see what’s present there.

cd 16385/ && ls

Whoa! We have just one table with just one row in mydatabase yet there are about 300 files present in this directory. These are mostly system catalogs that postgres cloned from the template database.

Now, let’s try to find the file for our table.

select relname, relfilenode, reltablespace from pg_class where relname = 'mytable';

We see the output as:

 relname | relfilenode | reltablespace 
---------+-------------+---------------
 mytable |       16390 |             0

The relfilenode is the file name for our table. If we go back to the data directory, the file 16390 contains the data that we inserted. But this is a binary file. At times, databases will apply some encoding or compression while storing data in files. As a result, the files are not directly readable- we can’t simply do cat <filename> and expect to read the entire contents. So how can we understand this data file and the file structure?

When postgres stores data, it doesn’t store one row or a few bytes. It thinks in terms of “pages” or “blocks”. Each block is given a fixed size of 8KB by default, though we can change this while setting up postgres. A file is made up of one or more such blocks. Naturally, it implies that size of each file will be in multiple of 8KB. Any data file of any database (even the system catalogs) are organized into blocks.

We can see that there seem to be several different files here- these are called “forks”. Each relation (i.e. table) can have upto four “forks”: | File | Fork | Purpose | |——|——|———| | {filenode} | main | Actual row data | | {filenode}_fsm | FSM | Free Space Map — tracks available space per page. Used for efficiency | | {filenode}_vm | VM | Visibility Map — tracks per-page visibility and freeze status. Used for concurrency control | | {filenode}_init | init | Unlogged tables/indexes only — template for reset after crash |

We can list the binary contents of the 16390 file by doing hexdump 16390. This isn’t very helpful ofcourse since it’s binary, but observe that at the beginning there are a few bytes written and there are a few bytes written at the end. We can decode this binary dump to see if we can interpret this.

The structure of a postgres data file looks something like the following:

As we can see, the table’s data is broken into “segments” of size 1GB ( this too is configurable ). For our table, if we had 4GB of data, the segment files will be named as: 16390, 16390.1, 16390.2, and 16390.3. Each segment file is made of one or more blocks. Each block has some headers, a slot array, and the rows. First block of a segment has some special headers as well. The slot array tells the offset for a row within the block. The slot array grows from the top while the rows grow from the bottom. The space in between them is the “free space” where new inserts can go.

Now that we know how the data is organized in a segment file, let’s see if we can interpret it. We won’t get into headers that much, but rather focus on the ItemIdData array and the tuple data.

Credits and Resources:

For this post, I have heavily used Claude Code. Along with that, I have relied on the following resources:

  1. Intro to Database Systems, CMU
  2. PostgreSQL Source Code

item.title: How Does Postgres Handle Connections?
item.description:
Postgres works on a client-server model. There is a Postgres server that is running an infinite loop listening for new, incoming requests. Clients wanting to interact with Postgres connect with this server.

How Does Postgres Handle Connections?

As we all know, postgres is an awesome, open source database system. In these series of blog posts, I am going to explore some internals of Postgres.

In this blog, we explore how postgres handles incoming connections and what implications it has for performance and scale. We’ll try to do a walkthrough of this using a postgres container and exploring some of the postgres source code.

Prerequisites

For this ( and subsequent ) posts, I am assuming that the reader:

  • Knows what docker containers are, how to build and run them.
  • Is familiar with the terms processes and threads

For this post, I am using a docker container for postgres and a docker container for a simple application connecting to postgres. Both files can be found here.

To build the containers, run:

# Build the postgres and the python application images
docker build -t postgres-17.6:v1 .
docker build -f Dockerfile.client -t pg-client:v1 .

# To let the python app talk to postgres, we create a docker network
docker network create pgnet

# Run the docker container for postgres
docker run -d --name postgres --network pgnet -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres-17.6:v1

Walkthrough

Now that we have the docker containers built, let’s begin the walkthrough.

Let’s exec into the postgres image:

docker exec -it postgres bash

Once inside, we can list all the processes running in our container by doing ps aux. We get the following output:

postgres@0f41997a8b1b:/$ ps aux
USER         PID %CPU %MEM    VSZ   RSS TTY      STAT START   TIME COMMAND
postgres       1  0.0  0.1 217536 28556 ?        Ss   Mar12   0:00 postgres
postgres      49  0.0  0.0 217668 10088 ?        Ss   Mar12   0:00 postgres: checkpointer 
postgres      50  0.0  0.0 217692  7436 ?        Ss   Mar12   0:00 postgres: background writer 
postgres      52  0.0  0.0 217536 10264 ?        Ss   Mar12   0:00 postgres: walwriter 
postgres      53  0.0  0.0 219112  9136 ?        Ss   Mar12   0:00 postgres: autovacuum launcher 
postgres      54  0.0  0.0 219120  8276 ?        Ss   Mar12   0:00 postgres: logical replication launcher 
postgres     399  1.3  0.0   7352  4096 pts/0    Ss   06:51   0:00 bash
postgres     406  0.0  0.0   9392  4116 pts/0    R+   06:51   0:00 ps aux

Already a lot seems to be going on, even though we have just freshly started the postgres server. There are several processes already running. We’ll get to the other processes later in the series, but for now the most important process for us is the one with PID 1. This is the postmaster. When we start postgres, the postmaster process is started. It then spawns the other postgres processes that we see listed above.

The postmaster process has a key responsibilty: it runs an infinite loop, waiting for new connections, and “handles” the incoming connections. Of course, there are other things as well that this postmaster process does, but for the purposes of this blog, we’ll focus on connection handling.

Now, let’s try to connect to postgres using the python application. Open a new terminal and run:

docker run --rm --network pgnet pg-client:v1 connect

This is going to run the python application that will try to connect to the postgres, wait for a few seconds and then shut down. From the postgres server terminal, if we again run ps aux, we get a new entry now, the process with PID 432:

postgres@0f41997a8b1b:/$ ps aux
USER         PID %CPU %MEM    VSZ   RSS TTY      STAT START   TIME COMMAND
postgres       1  0.0  0.1 217536 28556 ?        Ss   Mar12   0:00 postgres
postgres      49  0.0  0.0 217668 10088 ?        Ss   Mar12   0:00 postgres: checkpointer 
postgres      50  0.0  0.0 217692  7436 ?        Ss   Mar12   0:00 postgres: background writer 
postgres      52  0.0  0.0 217536 10264 ?        Ss   Mar12   0:00 postgres: walwriter 
postgres      53  0.0  0.0 219112  9136 ?        Ss   Mar12   0:00 postgres: autovacuum launcher 
postgres      54  0.0  0.0 219120  8276 ?        Ss   Mar12   0:00 postgres: logical replication launcher 
postgres     426  0.6  0.0   7352  4060 pts/0    Ss   06:57   0:00 bash
postgres     432  0.0  0.0 219648 12960 ?        Ss   06:57   0:00 postgres: myuser mydatabase 172.18.0.3(48278) idle
postgres     433  0.0  0.0   9392  4136 pts/0    R+   06:57   0:00 ps aux

When our python application tried to connect to postgres server, the postmaster process jumped to action and created a new process to handle that connection request. From the name of the process, we can interpret a few things:

  • postgres: - this is the prefix attached to all the processes spawned by postmaster
  • myuser - the name of the user that connected to postgres
  • mydatabase - the name of the database to which the user connected
  • 172.18.0.3(48278) - the host and port of the python application i.e. the client
  • idle - the state of the connection. Currently, the connection is sitting idle, without any work to do.

If we try to simulate a select query that runs for 30 seconds using:

docker run --rm --network pgnet pg-client:v1 select

we see the state of the connection change from idle to SELECT. This is postgres indicating to us that the handler process is currently executing a SELECT request sent by the client.

If we open another terminal and again try to connect to postgres server, we will see another process is being spawned. This is a key point: for every connection, the postgres server is going to have a process handling that connection. This process has its own stack, memory space, and the context switching overhead. At the same time, this process is entirely independent of the postgres server process. If the connection handling process crashes, there is no impact of it on the postgres server- it will continue to function as before.

Postgres runs on a multi-process parallelization model. For every new connection, postgres is going to spawn a new process to handle it. When the connection is terminated, the process is also killed. Now, most modern database are not going to follow multi-process model, but rather the multi-threaded model. For each new connection, they’re gonna spawn (reuse from the threadpool) some threads. This is lightweight than the process based approach but if not carefully designed, can cause the database to crash.

The multi-process model of postgres has important implications on how we scale postgres.

If we have an application we thousands of users who want to connect to the database, the postgres server is going to end up spawning thousands of processes. This is going to hamper the performance of our database. We simply cannot have a case where are spawning thousands of processes just to handle connections.

To get around this, we can do several things. The OpenAI blog post lists a bunch of things they did to scale postgres to serve 800 million users. We’ll focus on a couple of them:

  1. Setting max_connections parameter: at the most basic level, we can restrict the number of connections postgres will accept. By default, this is set to 100. After this limit is reached, the clients trying to connect will get an error. This safeguards the postgres server but doesn’t serve the clients well. So, we look at the next option.

  2. Using a load balancer like PgBouncer. In such a setup, the clients try to connect to the load balancer and the load balancer maintains a small pool of connections with postgres. As a result, from our application’s point of view, there could be thousands of connections but from the point of view of the database, there are only a handful of connections.

Credits and Resources:

For this post, I have heavily used Claude Code. Along with that, I have relied on the following resources:

  1. Intro to Database Systems by CMU
  2. Postgres Source Code
  3. You can also check out the youtube video I made on this post here.
